title: Vue v-memo: skipping DOM patch work
prerequisites: Basic understanding of the virtual DOM patch process

progressiveExplaining.eli5: Imagine a teacher taking attendance. Every morning she calls every student's name one by one, even the forty kids who were here yesterday and will be here today. v-memo is like a note she writes on each desk: 'This student was here and nothing about them changed — skip them.' On the next call, she only looks at the few desks without a note. She still checks the note every time, but she skips the slow part — asking each kid forty questions.
progressiveExplaining.junior: v-memo="[deps]" tells Vue: if every value in the deps array is identical (Object.is) since the last render, reuse the rendered virtual nodes of this block and skip the diff/patch entirely. Typical usage: v-for with v-memo="[item.id, item.updatedAt]" so a row only re-renders when its own data changed: <div v-for="item in items" :key="item.id" v-memo="[item.id, item.updatedAt]">. The deps array is compared with shallow equality against the previous render's values. When a dependency changes, the whole block re-renders and the memo caches the new values.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, v-memo is a patch-level bailout: when deps are unchanged, Vue skips the createVNode/patch recursive walk for that subtree entirely — no new vnodes, no diff, no DOM reads or writes for that block. This is a different lever from memoized components (which bail at the component boundary by comparing props); v-memo operates at the template block level and is especially useful inside v-for, where per-row components would be overkill or where rows are cheap but numerous. The trade-off is correctness: the memo condition is your responsibility. Any value that affects the subtree must be listed, or you get stale DOM — the classic trap is forgetting to include the reactive source that the block reads, so the UI stops updating.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: In the compiled render function, v-memo becomes an argument to createBlock or to the openBlock/block setup: the compiler emits the memo deps array as a runtime argument to the block's patch flag (PatchFlags.BAIL / dynamic props handling). At patch time, Vue's baseCreateRenderer compares the memoized deps (stored on the block vnode as patchFlag & shape) with the new deps using isMemoSame (a loop of Object.is comparisons). If equal, the vnode is reused as-is (the old vnode is returned and patching stops); if different, the normal mount/patch path runs and the memo is updated. Inside v-for, this effectively creates per-row memo slots in the fragment's dynamic children list, so unchanged rows cost one small array compare per row instead of a subtree diff.

interviewGotchas.question: When is v-memo the wrong tool compared to component-level memoization?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Interviewers use this to check whether the candidate understands the two bailout levels in Vue: component props comparison vs template-block memo.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: v-memo skips the vnode diff for a template block; memoized components skip the whole component render when props are shallowly equal. If the row itself is a component with expensive setup/effects, memo() on the component is the better lever because it avoids re-running the render function and lifecycle entirely. v-memo shines for large flat lists of cheap rows where component overhead per row would itself be wasteful. The wrong use is putting v-memo around a block that reads many reactive sources — the deps array grows, the compare cost approaches the patch cost, and you risk stale output if you miss a source.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The trap answer is 'v-memo is like memo()'. They operate at different layers — one is a template patch optimization, the other is a component render bailout — and v-memo has a correctness hazard memo() does not: memo() compares props automatically, while v-memo trusts your deps array completely. Missing a dependency silently freezes that part of the UI, which is the failure interviewers want you to name.

interviewGotchas.question: What happens under the hood when v-memo's deps match — what exactly is skipped?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This targets mechanical understanding of the renderer: does the candidate know the difference between vnode creation, diffing, and DOM patching?
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: When isMemoSame returns true, the renderer returns the old block vnode and skips the entire mount/patch branch for that subtree: no new vnodes are created, the diff (patchChildren with keyed or unkeyed comparison) never runs, and no DOM insert/update/remove is performed. The vnode is also marked so nested dynamic children are not re-traversed. The one cost that remains is the deps comparison itself — a shallow loop of Object.is over the array — which is O(deps) and trivially cheap. So a 1000-row list with one changed row costs 999 small array compares plus one real patch, versus 1000 full row patches.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The classic misunderstanding is that v-memo 'prevents re-renders of the component'. The component's render function still runs on parent updates (it must, to evaluate the deps array); only the subtree patch is skipped. Another trap: claiming it skips the reactive effect — v-memo does not change reactivity at all; it changes the renderer's patch decision. Candidates who say 'the reactive effect doesn't run' reveal they conflate the render/patch pipeline with reactivity tracking.
